messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin Keller, a 50-year-old psychologist in private practice, had spent most of his adult life relying on language. He was used to helping other people find words for fear, shame, and grief, and he had long understood himself as steady, thoughtful, and capable under pressure. The assault fractured that sense of himself in a way he still struggled to describe. Several months before seeking help, he had attended a professional gathering at a hotel bar after a training. He remembered the sharp smell of liquor on another man’s breath and clothing when the man followed him into a quieter corridor and then into a room. After that, Martin’s account thinned into fragments of bodily terror and humiliation. What remained most powerfully was not a coherent visual sequence but the sense of being handled, overpowered, and used. Even now, when he tried to tell the story, he would stop abruptly, his jaw tightening, as if he were pushing the memory away before it could fully form. He would say that he could feel the event in his body with full force, yet could not seem to put what happened into words.

In the weeks afterward, he returned to work and tried to continue seeing patients, telling himself that maintaining his schedule would prove he was still himself. Instead, ordinary moments in his office building began to undo him. If a patient came in carrying the faint smell of alcohol, or if sirens rose from the street below during session, he felt an immediate wave of discomfort that seemed out of proportion to what was happening around him. In those moments, what frightened him most was not only the surge itself but what it seemed to say about him. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him, that whatever had happened in that hotel had reduced him from a person with agency to an object something could be done to. The smell of alcohol or the cry of sirens did not just unsettle him; they seemed to confirm his bleakest conclusions that he was damaged, deadened, less than fully human now.

Those beliefs hardened quietly over time. Martin described feeling dead inside with his wife and in his office, as if some essential animating part of him had gone out. He increasingly judged every flinch, every unsettled moment, as evidence that the assault had permanently altered him. Holding that view made it harder for him to approach the memory directly. Whenever he sensed the event nearing consciousness, he cut it off before it was complete, almost reflexively, as though allowing the whole thing into words would seal the fact that he had become only an object in his own mind. He could sit with the emotional intensity of the assault—shame, dread, a sickening helplessness—without any clear image at all, and his inability to narrate it only deepened his conviction that he was no longer capable in the way he had once been.

The more inaccessible the memory felt, the more Martin took that as proof of damage rather than as a symptom of trauma. He noticed that when the event came back as a wordless flood—terror without pictures, bodily distress without a story—he felt especially stripped of personhood. Not being able to tell it, not being able to hold the memory from beginning to end, left him certain that the assault had erased something fundamental in him. Each failed attempt to recall it fully seemed to verify his sense that he was dead inside and had lost the abilities that once defined both his work and his identity.

By then, his fear had sharpened his attention to the world around him. Because he already believed he was irrevocably changed and vulnerable, he moved through his day scanning for anything that might signal another collapse: the stale scent of alcohol in the hallway outside his practice, a distant siren passing during an afternoon session, even the first subtle feeling of being uncomfortable in his own body. His appraisals made these cues loom larger and arrive faster. In his office, he began cracking a window in winter to clear the air, shortening sessions when city noise was heavy, and bracing himself before opening the waiting-room door. He understood the irony that, as a psychologist, he could recognize trauma responses in the abstract, yet from the inside it felt simpler and more damning: these reactions meant he was no longer who he had been.

At home, his wife experienced him as present but unreachable. He was not describing new conflicts so much as an absence; he sat beside her at dinner and felt hollow, unable to explain why a passing ambulance outside could leave him mute for the rest of the evening. What finally brought him to treatment was a recent session in which a patient mentioned meeting friends at a bar. Martin caught the smell of alcohol from the man’s coat, felt the now-familiar jolt of discomfort, and lost his train of thought entirely. For the first time in his career, he worried in the moment that he could not do his job. Seeking help felt humiliating, but also necessary. He said he was afraid that if this continued, the assault would define him more completely than his own life had. What he wanted, cautiously and without much confidence, was to feel like a person again and to be able to face what happened without disappearing from himself.
